--- title: "Positron" subtitle: "Extended course – day 1" format: revealjs # Session 5 of day 1 of the Extended course, the same for every case: the IDE # taught live in the workspace of the housing-audit case, with Positron on the # shared screen and RStudio and VS Code users following in their own IDE. # Four sections: the folder and the window, running code, data, plots and # help, the terminal and other IDEs. The screenshots come from the module # tools/ide.qmd. One optional slide stays on the d toggle (run "ide"): the # Command Palette. core-runs: [] --- ## {#overview .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.todaymeta} Session 5 of 6 on day 1, the same for every case ::: :::: {.todaybox} ::: {.nonincremental .fs-85} 1. The folder and the window – the workspace opened as a folder, and the parts of the window 2. Running code – a script as a whole, a statement at a time and in part, the console, and the objects of the session 3. Data, plots and help – the Data Explorer, the Plots pane, the Viewer and the help pages 4. The terminal and other IDEs – the command line inside the IDE, and where the same things sit in RStudio and VS Code ::: :::: ::: {.todaytake .fs-85} You leave knowing what each part of your IDE is for, and able to run, inspect and look at the work of the workspace without leaving it ::: ::: {.todaymeta} Positron on the shared screen, in the workspace of the housing-audit case; RStudio and VS Code users follow in their own IDE ::: ::: notes The last session used your IDE as a place to type. This one is about the IDE itself, and it names Positron throughout, because Positron is the IDE of the course and the one on my screen. If you work in RStudio or VS Code, stay there: every step has its counterpart, and one slide in the last section says where each thing sits. There are four sections. First the folder and the window: how the workspace opens and what each part of the window is for. Then running code, from a whole script to a part of one statement, and the objects that the session holds once the code has run. Then the places where you look at things, the data, the plots and the help pages. And last the terminal, the other IDEs, and what to do when the window misbehaves. ::: ## Editors and IDEs {#where-you-write-it} ::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 5"}
PositronThe IDE of the course, from Posit, built on the open-source core of VS Code. R and Python as equals.
RStudioStill excellent, still supported. If it is what you know, use it.
VS CodeDoes anything, once configured. Many extensions.
JupyterNotebook-first. Cells can run out of order.
NeovimFor the keyboard only. Steep to learn, and very fast once learned.
::: ::: {.fragment .small .fs-80} Of the choices in the toolchain, the editor matters least. It changes how *you* work and nothing about what a reader receives. **A trap:** a tool that runs code piece by piece lets you run the pieces out of order, so it can show output that no clean run would produce. Restart and run everything before you believe it. ::: ::: {.src} Positron and RStudio are both from Posit; both are free, and RStudio is open source. ::: ::: notes The editor is the least consequential choice in the toolchain, so I will be quick. Positron is the newer environment from Posit, built on the open-source core of VS Code, with R and Python as equals, and it is what I drive on the shared screen. RStudio is still excellent and still supported, and if it is what you know, there is no reason to move. VS Code will do anything once you have configured it. Jupyter is notebook-first and Python-first, and Neovim is for people who never want to touch a mouse. What matters is the trap in the second box, which applies to every tool in which you run code a piece at a time, the console of an IDE included: you can run the pieces out of order, so the output on your screen may be output that no clean run would ever produce. Restart the session and run everything from the top before you believe a number. ::: # The folder and the window {#the-folder-and-the-window .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Section 1 ::: ::: notes Section one is about the shape of the window. Positron works on a folder, so we start by opening the folder of the workspace and letting R start inside it. Then the seven parts of the window, under the names by which the documentation of Positron describes each part, so that you can find a pane when I name it. Then the files of the workspace, what each file is for and which files you can leave alone, and a first task in which you do all of this on your own machine. ::: ## Opening the folder {#opening-the-folder .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="56%"} ::: {.small} - **File → Open Folder…** (Ctrl+K, then Ctrl+O), and select the folder `replication-lab-housing-main` itself, not a file inside it - The Explorer lists the files of the folder, and R starts in a console whose **working directory** is that folder, so that `data/housing_audit.csv` finds the file - The button at the top right names the R that runs the session, with a circle that is green while R is idle and blue while it is busy ::: ::: ::: {.column width="44%"} ![](../tools/images/ide/02-file-open-folder.png){fig-alt="The File menu of Positron, with Open Folder highlighted beside its shortcut Ctrl+K Ctrl+O." height="400px" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: :::: ::: notes Positron works on a folder, and the course works in one folder, the unzipped workspace. File, Open Folder, or Control and K followed by Control and O, then choose the folder itself rather than a file inside it, and press Select Folder. Two things happen at once. The files of the folder appear in the Explorer on the left, and R starts in a console whose working directory is that folder, so that a path such as data slash housing audit dot csv finds its file without further ado. Positron starts R by itself when the folder holds R files, and the workspace does. The button at the top right of the window, the interpreter picker, names the version of R that runs your code, which is the first thing to check when a result differs from the one in the course. RStudio users open the dot Rproj file instead, which does the same. ::: ## The parts of the window {#the-parts-of-the-window .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="74%"} ![](../tools/images/ide/07-window-parts.png){fig-alt="The whole Positron window with seven parts outlined and numbered: the Activity Bar, the Explorer, the editor with the working script, the Console under it, the Variables and Plots panes on the right, the interpreter picker at the top and the Status Bar at the bottom." style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: ::: {.column width="26%"} ::: {.fs-70 .nonincremental} 1. **Activity Bar** – switches the side bar 2. **Primary Side Bar** – the Explorer, with the files 3. **Editor** – a tab for each open file 4. **Panel** – the Console, beside the Terminal 5. **Secondary Side Bar** – Variables, Plots, Help, Viewer 6. **Top Bar** – search, and the interpreter picker 7. **Status Bar** – Quarto, the cursor, the language ::: ::: :::: ::: notes This is the whole window with the workspace open, as it looks after the steps of the next section, with its seven parts numbered as the documentation of Positron names them. The strip of icons down the far left, the Activity Bar, switches what the side bar beside it shows, most of the time the Explorer with your files. The editor fills the middle, with a tab for each open file. Under it, the Panel holds the Console, in which R runs, beside the Terminal. On the right, the Secondary Side Bar holds the views of the R session: the Variables and Plots panes, and the Help and Viewer tabs. Along the top run the search box and the interpreter picker, and along the bottom the Status Bar. RStudio users will recognise their four panes: the editor does the work of the Source pane, and the Variables pane that of the Environment tab. ::: ## The files of the workspace {#the-files-of-the-workspace .smaller} ::: {.small} - `index.qmd` – the report, with Tasks 1 to 5 of the exercise and the preregistration block - `working_script.R` – the same steps as a plain script, for working in the console - `R/` – the check script, the starter file of the causal graph, and the helpers of Tasks 4 and 5 - `data/` – the data of the field experiment in which the original authors (OAs) emailed public housing authorities in the United States [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect], each file beside its codebook - `prep/` – a script that runs all five reanalyses of Task 3 at once - The rest can be left alone: `_freeze/`, `.github/`, `.devcontainer/` and the `.Rproj` file, which serve the route to a repository of your own and to RStudio ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Every part of the window can be resized by dragging its edge, and hidden and shown again: Ctrl+B for the side bar on the left, Ctrl+Alt+B for the one on the right, Ctrl+J for the Panel. ::: ::: notes The Explorer shows the workspace as you received it. index dot qmd is the report, with the five tasks of the exercise of the case and the preregistration block, and the last session of today takes it apart. working script dot R holds the same steps as a plain script, for working in the console. The R folder holds the check script, the starter file for the causal graph and the helpers of the later tasks, and the data folder holds the data files of the case, each beside its codebook. The prep folder holds a script that runs all five reanalyses of Task 3 at once. The rest serves the route from the workspace to a repository of your own, and can be left alone. [advance] Sooner or later you will hide a part of the window by accident, so it is worth knowing the three keys that bring the parts back. ::: ## Hands-on 1 – The folder and the window {#hands-on-1-the-folder-and-the-window .smaller} ::: {.small} 1. Open the folder of the workspace, and wait for the console to report that R has started 2. In the Explorer, unfold `data` and `R`. Click `working_script.R` once, and then double-click it, so that it stays open 3. Press Ctrl+J twice, to hide the Panel and bring it back 4. Click the interpreter picker at the top right, read which R runs your code, and press Esc ::: ::: {.fragment .small} RStudio or VS Code: open the folder in your IDE, and find the files, the console and the version of R. ::: ::: notes Your turn. Open the folder, if you have not already, and wait until the console says that R has started. Unfold the data and R folders in the Explorer. Click the working script once and notice that the name on its tab is in italics, which marks a preview that the next file you click will replace; double-click it, or start typing in it, to keep it open. Press Control and J twice, to hide the Panel and bring it back. And click the interpreter picker to read which R runs your code, then press Escape. [advance] If you work in RStudio or VS Code, do the same in your own IDE: open the folder, and find the files, the console and the version of R. Take the time you need. ::: # Running code {#running-code .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Section 2 ::: ::: notes Section two is about running code, which is most of what you do in an IDE. A script can run as a whole, a statement at a time, or in part, and we take each of the three on the files of the workspace. Then we look at the console, where the code runs, and at the Variables pane, which shows what the session holds once it has run. The task at the end finishes with a restart of R, which is the quickest test of whether a script recreates everything that it uses. ::: ## A script as a whole {#a-script-as-a-whole .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.small} - The run button at the top left of the editor runs **Source R File with Echo** (Ctrl+Shift+Enter), which prints each line before its result - The small arrow beside it offers **Source R File**, which runs the file with `source()` and prints the results only - On `R/check_setup.R`, Source R File prints an `[OK]` line for each check, the verdict 11 OK and 0 FAIL, and "You are ready" ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ![](../tools/images/ide/10-run-menu.png){fig-alt="The run menu of an R script, offering Source R File with Echo with the shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Enter, Source R File, and Execute Code with the shortcut Ctrl+Enter." width="100%" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: :::: ::: notes The whole file runs from the run button at the top left of the editor. The button itself runs Source R File with Echo, which prints every line of code in the console before its result, and the small arrow beside it opens a menu that also offers Source R File, which runs the file with source and prints the results only. The second suits the check script, whose code you do not need to read in the console, and it does the same as typing source R slash check setup dot R there. The check prints an OK line for each thing that the course needs, and its last check fits the reference specification of the housing-audit case, which must come out at minus nineteen point nine seven percentage points. The check script of every workspace works in the same way. ::: ## A statement at a time {#a-statement-at-a-time .smaller} ::: {.small} Lines 38 to 43 of `working_script.R`, run with one press of **Ctrl+Enter** with the cursor anywhere in them: ::: ```r audit |> datawizard::data_summary(emails = n(), bounced = sum(is.na(reply)), delivered = sum(!is.na(reply)), replies = sum(reply %in% 1), coded = sum(!is.na(named))) ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` emails | bounced | delivered | replies | coded ---------------------------------------------- 1014 | 23 | 991 | 563 | 558 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Ctrl+Enter sends the **statement** under the cursor, however many lines it runs over, and moves the cursor on to the next statement, so that pressing it again and again steps through the script. ::: ::: notes Ctrl and Enter is the key that you will press most often. With the cursor in a script, it sends the statement under the cursor to the console and moves the cursor down to the next statement. Click at the start of line thirty and press it: R reads the data into audit, and the cursor moves to line thirty-one. Press it again and R loads the helpers of the exercise, and the cursor jumps over the comments to line thirty-eight. Press it once more and the whole statement of lines thirty-eight to forty-three runs, because a statement is a complete piece of R code and may run over several lines. The console prints the counts: a thousand and fourteen emails, twenty-three bounced, nine hundred and ninety-one delivered, five hundred and sixty-three replies, and five hundred and fifty-eight replies with a greeting code. [advance] Pressing the key again and again therefore steps through the script in order. ::: ## Part of a statement {#part-of-a-statement .smaller} ::: {.small} Select from `audit` on line 47 to the closing bracket of `data_filter()` on line 48, without the `|>` after it, and press **Ctrl+Enter**: ::: ```r audit |> datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) ``` ::: {.fs-90} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 991 × 16 email_id name group name_sex hard_email reply reply24 named * 1 1 Shani… black female 0 0 NA NA 2 2 Brett white male 1 1 1 0 3 3 Shani… black female 0 1 1 1 4 4 Tyrone black male 1 1 0 0 5 6 Gabri… hisp… female 1 1 1 1 6 7 Shani… black female 1 0 NA NA 7 8 Santi… hisp… male 0 1 1 0 8 9 Brett white male 0 1 1 1 9 10 Brett white male 1 1 1 1 10 11 Shani… black female 0 1 1 0 # ℹ 981 more rows # ℹ 8 more variables: hispanic_official , waitlist , # white_third , black_third , hispanic_third , # pop_third , poverty_third , # assessment_third ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: notes With a selection, Control and Enter sends exactly the text that you selected, which lets you run one part of a statement, such as the first steps of a pipe, to look at the data at that point. Select from audit at the start of line forty-seven to the closing bracket of data filter on line forty-eight, leaving out the pipe that follows it, and press the key. The console prints the nine hundred and ninety-one delivered emails as a tibble, the kind of data frame that readr creates, with its first ten rows and a note of how many more rows and columns there are. This is how you take apart a long chain that gives a surprising result: run it a step at a time, and look at what each step hands to the next. ::: ## The console {#the-console .smaller} ![](../tools/images/ide/15-console.png){fig-alt="The console of Positron. Its header bar shows the path of the workspace folder and buttons to restart R, clear the console and show information. nrow(audit) prints 1014, names(audit) prints the sixteen column names, and getwd() prints the path of the folder replication-lab-housing-main." width="92%" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: {.small} - `>` means that R is waiting, `+` that a statement is not finished. The Up arrow brings back earlier commands, and Ctrl+L clears the screen and keeps every object - The circular arrow in the bar restarts R (Ctrl+Shift+0), and every object goes with the old session. Positron does not save the objects of a session for the next time ::: ::: notes The console shows a greater-than sign when R is waiting for you and a plus sign at the start of each further line of a statement that runs over several lines. You can type into it directly, and the Up arrow brings back the commands that you ran before, so that a line can be run again or changed without being retyped. Control and L clears what the console shows and leaves every object in place. The bar at the top shows the working directory of the session, which should be the folder of the workspace, as getwd confirms here. The circular arrow restarts R, which ends the session, and every object goes with it. Positron does not save the objects of a session when it closes, and that suits the course: a result is reproducible only when the script recreates every object that it uses. ::: ## The Variables pane {#the-variables-pane .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="48%"} ::: {.small} - The objects of the session, in three groups: **DATA**, **VALUES** and **FUNCTIONS** - A data frame unfolds into its columns, each with a preview, its type and its length - The grid icon beside a data frame opens it in the Data Explorer ::: ::: ::: {.column width="52%"} ![](../tools/images/ide/16-variables-pane.png){fig-alt="The Variables pane, with audit described as 1014 rows by 16 columns and unfolded into its columns, from email_id to waitlist, each with a preview of its values, its type and its length." width="100%" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: :::: ::: notes The Variables pane, in the Session tab on the right, lists the objects of the session in three groups, data frames under data, other values under values, and functions under functions. Each line gives the name of an object and a short preview of what it holds, and a data frame unfolds into its columns, each with its type and its length, so that the sixteen columns of audit appear with numbers marked dbl, text marked str, and every column a thousand and fourteen long. The Filter box at the top narrows the list, which helps once the helpers of the workspace have added their functions to it. And the small grid icon beside each data frame opens it in the Data Explorer, which the next section takes up. In RStudio the same list is the Environment pane. ::: ## Hands-on 2 – Running the workspace {#hands-on-2-running-the-workspace .smaller} ::: {.small} 1. Open `R/check_setup.R` and run it with **Source R File**, from the arrow beside the run button 2. In `working_script.R`, click at the start of line 30 and press Ctrl+Enter three times: the data, the helpers, then the counts 3. Select the first part of the pipe on lines 47 and 48, and press Ctrl+Enter 4. Restart R with Ctrl+Shift+0, watch the Variables pane empty, and run line 30 again ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The counts: 1,014 emails, 23 bounced, 991 delivered, 563 replies and 558 replies with a greeting code. ::: ::: notes Your turn, and this time all three ways of running code. Run the check script as a whole with Source R File, and read its OK lines. Then step through the beginning of the working script with Control and Enter: the data, the helpers, the counts. Select the first part of the pipe that follows and run only that. And then restart R, with Control, Shift and zero or the circular arrow, and watch the Variables pane empty, because that is what a fresh session looks like and what a render of the report starts from. Run line thirty again to bring the data back. In RStudio and VS Code, Control and Enter does the same from the editor. Take the time you need. [advance] Check your counts against these. ::: # Data, plots and help {#data-plots-and-help .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Section 3 ::: ::: notes Section three is about the places in which you look at things. The Data Explorer shows a data frame as a grid, with a summary of every column beside it, and it is the part of Positron that most changes how it feels to look at data. Then the Plots pane, where every figure lands, the Viewer, which shows tables and web pages, and the help pages of R, which are better reading than most people expect. The task at the end is a look at the data of the case, of the kind that should come before any model. ::: ## The Data Explorer {#the-data-explorer .smaller} ![](../tools/images/ide/17-data-explorer.png){fig-alt="The Data Explorer showing audit in a tab of the editor: on the left the summary panel lists the sixteen columns with small charts and the share of missing values, and on the right the grid shows the first rows. The status line at the bottom reads 1,014 rows, 16 columns." width="88%" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: {.small} It opens from the grid icon in the Variables pane, from `View(audit)` in the console, or from a CSV file clicked in the Explorer. Ctrl+B, Ctrl+J and Ctrl+Alt+B give it the whole window. ::: ::: notes The Data Explorer shows a data frame as a grid of cells, much like a spreadsheet, with summary statistics for every column beside it. It opens from the grid icon in the Variables pane, from View of audit in the console, the call that RStudio users know, and from a CSV file clicked in the Explorer, which it reads without loading the file into R. Three parts make it up. The grid shows the cells, with the name and type of each column at its head. The summary panel on the left lists the columns, each with a small chart of its values and the share of missing values. And the filter bar above the grid and the summary panel holds filters on the rows. The default layout gives it little room, so I hide the other parts of the window while I look, as in this screenshot. ::: ## Summaries and filters {#summaries-and-filters .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="34%"} ![](../tools/images/ide/18-summary-panel.png){fig-alt="Two columns unfolded in the summary panel of the Data Explorer: name, with six unique values and none missing, and reply, with 23 missing values, a minimum of 0, a median of 1, a mean of 0.5681, a maximum of 1 and a standard deviation of 0.4956." height="470px" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: ::: {.column width="66%"} ::: {.small} - A column unfolds into a fuller summary: `reply` has 23 missing values, the bounced emails, and a mean of 0.5681, the reply rate - **+** in the filter bar adds a filter, and the menu at the head of a column sorts it. Filtered to Santiago and sorted by `reply`, the status line reads "Showing 207 rows (20.41% of 1,014 total)" - Filters change the view and leave the data alone: `nrow(audit)` still gives 1014 - **Convert to Code** writes the view as dplyr code; the course writes it with datawizard ::: ::: {.fs-85} ```r audit |> datawizard::data_filter(name == "Santiago") |> datawizard::data_arrange("-reply") ``` ::: ::: :::: ::: notes A column in the summary panel unfolds into a fuller summary. The column of names has six unique values and none missing, and reply has twenty-three missing values, the bounced emails, with a mean of point five six eight, which is the share of the delivered emails that received a reply. The plus sign in the filter bar adds a filter on the rows, and the menu at the head of each column sorts it. Filtered to the emails signed Santiago and sorted by reply, the status line at the bottom says that two hundred and seven rows are on display out of a thousand and fourteen. Filters and sorts change only what you look at, while the object in the session stays as it was. Convert to Code writes the code that reproduces the view, in dplyr, and the course writes the same steps with datawizard. ::: ## Plots and the Viewer {#plots-and-the-viewer .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.fs-80} ```r tinyplot::tinyplot(~ name, data = audit, type = "barplot") ``` ::: ![](../tools/images/ide/20-plots-pane.png){fig-alt="The Plots pane with a bar chart of the count of emails for each of the six names, and a toolbar of buttons for the previous and next plot, saving, copying, zoom and sizing." width="88%" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.fs-80} ```r audit |> datawizard::data_summary(emails = n(), replies = sum(reply %in% 1), by = "name") |> tinytable::tt() ``` ::: ![](../tools/images/ide/22-viewer-pane.png){fig-alt="The Viewer tab showing a table made with tinytable, with the columns name, emails and replies for each of the six names." width="88%" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: :::: ::: notes Every figure that R draws in the session appears in the Plots pane, under the Variables pane, labelled with the version of R that drew it and its number in the history of the session. The arrows at the top move back and forth through that history, and the other buttons save the plot to a file, copy it, zoom it, and open it in a window of its own. In the default sizing the figure is drawn to fit the pane, so widening the pane by dragging its edge gives a larger and clearer plot. The Viewer shows output that is a web page rather than text or a plot, such as a table made with tinytable, an interactive figure or the preview of a Quarto document, which the next session uses. RStudio has the same two tabs, in the pane at the bottom right. ::: ## Help pages {#help-pages .smaller} ```r ?datawizard::data_filter ``` ::: {.small} - `?` and the name of a function open its help page in the Help tab, on the right of the window, with working links and back and forward buttons - **F1** with the cursor on the name of a function in the editor does the same - A function written with its package opens its help page even when the package is not loaded - A page sets out what the function does, how it is called and what each argument means, and most pages end with examples that you can run ::: ::: notes The help pages of R are better than their reputation. A question mark followed by the name of a function opens its page in the Help tab, as a formatted page with working links, and the back and forward buttons return to the pages that you read before. F1, with the cursor on the name of a function in the editor, does the same without typing anything, and because every function in the course is written with its package, its page opens even when the package is not loaded. The page for data filter documents data match and data filter together, because datawizard describes the two functions on one page. Read the description and the arguments first, and then look for the examples near the end of the page, which you can copy into the console and run. ::: ## Hands-on 3 – Looking at the data {#hands-on-3-looking-at-the-data .smaller} ::: {.small} 1. Open `audit` in the Data Explorer, from the grid icon in the Variables pane, and unfold `name` and `reply` in the summary panel 2. Filter the view to the emails signed Santiago, sort it by `reply`, descending, and then run `nrow(audit)` in the console 3. Draw the bar chart of the emails by name, and find **Save Plot** in the Plots pane 4. Run `?datawizard::data_filter`, then put the cursor on `read_csv` in line 30 of the script and press F1 ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The filtered view shows 207 rows, and `nrow(audit)` still prints 1014. In RStudio, `View(audit)` opens the data viewer, and plots and help appear in the pane at the bottom right. ::: ::: notes Your turn, and the habit behind it is the most useful one of the day, which is to look at the data before any model is fitted. Open audit in the Data Explorer and unfold the two columns. Filter the view to Santiago, sort it by reply, and then check in the console that the data frame itself has not changed. Draw the bar chart of the emails by name, and find the button that saves a plot, which you will need when a figure goes into a document of your own. And open two help pages, one with the question mark and one with F1 from the script. If you work in RStudio or VS Code, use the data viewer, the plots and the help of your own IDE. Take the time you need. [advance] The view shows two hundred and seven rows, and the data frame is unchanged. ::: # The terminal and other IDEs {#the-terminal-and-other-ides .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Section 4 ::: ::: notes Section four collects what remains. The terminal is a command line inside the IDE, which the course uses for little, but which renders the report in the next session. The Command Palette is a search box for everything that Positron can do. Then one slide on where the same things sit in RStudio and in VS Code, for those of you who work there, and one on what to do when something in the window goes wrong. The last task ends where the next session begins. ::: ## The terminal {#the-terminal .smaller} ![](../tools/images/ide/23-terminal.png){fig-alt="The Terminal tab of the Panel in PowerShell, with a prompt that ends in the path of the folder replication-lab-housing-main. quarto --version prints a version number, and ls R lists check_setup.R, dag_starter.R and spec_tools.R." width="90%" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: {.small} - **Terminal → New Terminal** opens a command line in the folder of the workspace: PowerShell on Windows, the shell of the system on a Mac or under Linux - It speaks the language of the operating system, not R: `quarto --version` checks that Quarto is installed, and `ls R` lists a folder - In PowerShell, `R` on its own repeats earlier commands, so ask R for its version in the console, with `R.version.string` ::: ::: notes The Terminal tab of the Panel is a command line that starts in the folder of the workspace, and it speaks the language of the operating system rather than R: PowerShell on Windows, and normally the default shell of the system on a Mac or under Linux. The course uses it for little. It is where you check that Quarto is installed, with quarto dash dash version, and where quarto render runs when you render the report from the command line, which you will do at the end of the next session. One trap on Windows: in PowerShell the letter R typed on its own is a shortcut for a command that repeats earlier commands, so R dash dash version answers with an error instead of the version of R. The console is the place to ask R about itself. Click Console in the Panel to go back to R. ::: ## The Command Palette {#the-command-palette .smaller .deepdive run="ide"} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.small} - **Ctrl+Shift+P** opens a search box for every command of Positron, each with its keyboard shortcut beside it - Commands are grouped by a prefix: **Interpreter:** for the R sessions, **View:** for the layout, **Git:** for version control - **Ctrl+P** opens the same box for the files of the folder ::: ::: ::: {.column width="55%"} ![](../tools/images/ide/27-command-palette.png){fig-alt="The Command Palette with the text interpreter typed into it, listing the commands that begin with Interpreter, among them Restart Active Interpreter Session with the shortcut Ctrl+Shift+0." width="100%" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: :::: ::: notes Everything that Positron can do is a command, and the Command Palette is a search box for all of them. You type a few letters of what you want, such as interpreter, restart or render, and the matching commands appear, each with its keyboard shortcut beside it, so that the palette also teaches you the shortcuts as you go. Commands are grouped by a prefix: Interpreter for the R sessions, View for the layout, Git for version control, among others. Control and P opens the same box for files instead, and a few letters of a file name are enough to find it. When I name a command on the slides of this course, such as Interpreter: Restart Active Interpreter Session, this is where you type it. ::: ## RStudio and VS Code {#rstudio-and-vs-code .smaller} ::: {.fs-70} | | Positron | RStudio | VS Code | |---|---|---|---| | **Open the workspace** | File → Open Folder… | the `.Rproj` file | File → Open Folder… | | **Run a line or a selection** | Ctrl+Enter | Ctrl+Enter | Ctrl+Enter | | **Run the whole file** | Source R File | Source, or Ctrl+Shift+S | Ctrl+Shift+S | | **The console** | the Panel, under the editor | the pane at the bottom left | an R terminal, from **R: Create R terminal** | | **The objects of the session** | Variables pane | Environment pane | the R icon in the Activity Bar | | **Data, plots and help** | Data Explorer, Plots pane, Help tab | `View()`, and the Plots and Help tabs at the bottom right | `View()`, a plot viewer, and help in a tab beside the editor | | **Render the report** | Preview | Render | Preview, with Quarto installed | ::: ::: {.small} On a Mac, Cmd takes the place of Ctrl in most shortcuts. The Mac steps are untested, and the course offers no help with a Mac in class. ::: ::: notes For those of you who work in another IDE, this is where the same things sit. RStudio opens the workspace as a project, from the dot Rproj file, which sets the working directory to the folder. Control and Enter runs the current line or the selection in all three IDEs. The whole file runs from the Source button in RStudio, and from Control, Shift and S in RStudio and VS Code. RStudio keeps the console at the bottom left and the objects in the Environment pane, and plots and help appear in the tabs at the bottom right. VS Code runs R in a terminal, which the command R: Create R terminal starts, and shows the objects of the session under the R icon in the Activity Bar. To render the report, RStudio has a Render button, and VS Code a Preview command, which needs Quarto installed on its own. ::: ## When something goes wrong {#when-something-goes-wrong .smaller} ::: {.fs-75} | Problem | What to do | |---|---| | `'data/housing_audit.csv' does not exist in current working directory` | Positron has no folder open, or another one. Check the path at the top of the console, and open the folder of the workspace | | Ctrl+Enter does nothing, or adds a new line | Click in the code first. A new file runs as R only once it is saved with the extension `.R` | | R stays busy and does not finish | **Interpreter: Interrupt Active Interpreter Session**. If R does not answer, restart it and run the script from the top | | A number differs from the one in the course | Restart R and run the script from the top, and check which R runs the session | | A part of the window has disappeared | Ctrl+B, Ctrl+Alt+B or Ctrl+J, or **View: Reset View Locations** | | The window behaves oddly | **Developer: Reload Window**, which restarts the interface and keeps the R session | ::: ::: notes Most of what goes wrong in the IDE during the course falls into a handful of cases. A file that does not exist in the current working directory almost always means that no folder is open, or the wrong one, so check the path at the top of the console and open the folder of the workspace. Control and Enter doing nothing usually means that the cursor is not in the editor, or that a new file has not yet been saved as an R file. If R stays busy, interrupt it from the Command Palette, and restart it if it does not answer. A number that differs from the one in the course usually comes from an object left over from earlier work, so restart and run from the top. And a window that behaves oddly can be reloaded without losing the R session. Problems with the installation itself are on the Setup help page. ::: ## Hands-on 4 – The terminal and the palette {#hands-on-4-the-terminal-and-the-palette .smaller} ::: {.small} 1. **Terminal → New Terminal**, then type `quarto --version` and press Enter, and `ls R` 2. Click **Console** in the Panel to go back to R 3. Press Ctrl+Shift+P, type `interpreter`, find the shortcut of **Interpreter: Restart Active Interpreter Session**, and press Esc 4. Press Ctrl+P, type `check` and press Enter, which opens `R/check_setup.R` ::: ::: {.fragment .small} If `quarto --version` prints no version, tell me now: the next session renders the report, and Quarto has to be found first. ::: ::: notes The last task of the session. Open a terminal from the Terminal menu, ask Quarto for its version, and list the R folder of the workspace, which holds the three scripts that you have already met. Then click Console to go back to R. Open the Command Palette, type interpreter, and find the shortcut of the command that restarts the session, which you will use at the end of the next session, and press Escape. And open the check script with Control and P and a few letters of its name. [advance] One thing matters for what comes next. If quarto dash dash version does not print a version, tell me now, because the next session renders the report, and the render needs Quarto. Take the time you need. ::: ## The next session and the reading {#next-session} ::: {.small .nonincremental} - **The next session** takes up Quarto: the report of the workspace taken apart, from what a `.qmd` file holds to a render from a clean session. <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
